---
title: "Quiz: Calibration and unknown samples"
---

[Exercises](19-calibration.qmd) · [Lecture slides](../lectures/19-calibration/lec.qmd)

Try each question before opening its hint or answer.

---

**Q1.** Known concentration is in mg/L; the measured response is absorbance.
Which formula fits the calibration used here?

(i) `lm(absorbance ~ concentration_mg_l, data = standards)`  

(ii) `lm(concentration_mg_l ~ absorbance, data = standards)`

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
The response is left of `~`; the predictor is right of it.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
(i). Prepared concentration is the predictor and absorbance the response.
The unknown concentration is later estimated by rearranging that fitted line.
:::

---

**Q2.** For `absorbance = 0.04 + 0.065 * concentration_mg_l`, estimate
concentration from an in-range reading of 0.30. What does the slope mean?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Rearrange to `(reading - intercept) / slope`.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$(0.30-0.04)/0.065 = 4$ **mg/L**. The slope is an increase of 0.065
absorbance per mg/L increase in concentration.
:::

---

**Q3.** A standard has observed absorbance 0.30 and fitted absorbance 0.28.
What is its residual, and where is its point relative to the line?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Residual = observed − fitted.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The residual is **+0.02 absorbance**, so the point lies above the fitted
line. It is a signal-scale difference, not a concentration.
:::

---

**Q4.** Measured standard signals span 0.024–0.525. Unknown X1 reads 0.270
and X2 reads 0.700. Which gets a supported inverse estimate, and how should
the other appear in the saved table?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Check the measured signal range before inverting.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
X1 is in range. Retain X2's ID and reading with an out-of-range flag and
a missing concentration estimate. A suitable new measurement is needed.
:::

---

**Q5.** A new sample is diluted from 1.00 mL to 10.00 mL total volume. Its
new in-range reading corresponds to 7.40 mg/L. Estimate the original concentration
assuming no measured substance is lost or reacts.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Multiply the diluted estimate by final total volume / original-sample volume.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$7.40\times(10.00/1.00) = 74.0$ **mg/L** using the rounded estimate.
This uses a measured dilution and stated volumes; it does not validate a
different sample's out-of-range reading.
:::
